title: Missing Meroke Village Marker, Merrick
summary: A former New York State historic marker in Merrick acknowledged a Meroke village area. It is no longer standing, but its text keeps local memory of Meroke presence visible.
address_label: Sunrise Highway vicinity, west of Central Boulevard, Merrick
ancestral_territory_note: Meroke is one of the historical forms associated with the Merrick name.
why_this_matters: The missing Meroke marker shows how Native place history can be acknowledged in one generation and fade from the roadside landscape in another. Restoring the story helps reconnect Merrick to Meroke presence while treating village places with respect.
introduction_content:
A New York State historical marker once stood near Sunrise Highway in Merrick, commemorating a Meroke village. The sign has been missing for many years, but its recorded inscription preserves a public acknowledgment of the community for whom Merrick is named.1

The Former Marker’s Words

SITE OF
INDIAN VILLAGE
LODGES OF MEROKE TRIBE
WERE FEW HUNDRED FEET
SOUTH. MERRICK SETTLED
IN 1643.

The wording survives in the New York historical marker listing, entry 1299. The sign itself has been missing for many years.
history_content:
What the missing sign remembered

The sign’s reference to 1643 linked a Native village with the beginning of English settlement. Merriack also appears in the surviving Hempstead deed tradition, alongside Masepeage and Rockaway. These names place Native people within the historical record as participants in agreements, rather than as an unnamed population before the town began.2

The story continued after that date. Tackapousha challenged payment for Mercock land in 1675, and Horton’s Merrick journal records a Native community in 1742. The marker’s disappearance therefore obscures a history much longer than the single year on its face. The neighboring articles let readers follow landholding, community life, and public memory beyond the lost sign.34
preservation_content: The missing marker shows how Native place history can be acknowledged in one generation and fade from the roadside landscape in another. Restoring the story through careful interpretation and local sources helps reconnect Merrick to Meroke presence while treating village places with respect.
